title: MYASTHENIC SYNDROME, CONGENITAL, 11, ASSOCIATED WITH ACETYLCHOLINE RECEPTOR DEFICIENCY

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital myasthenic syndrome-11 associated with acetylcholine receptor deficiency (CMS11) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding rapsyn (RAPSN; 601592) on chromosome 11p11.2.

checks.claim: Congenital myasthenic syndrome-11 associated with acetylcholine receptor deficiency (CMS11) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the RAPSN gene, which encodes rapsyn.
checks.evidence_quote: we identify three recessive rapsyn mutations: one patient carries L14P in TPR1 and N88K in TPR3; two are homozygous for N88K; and one carries N88K and 553ins5
checks.explanation: Paper shows homozygous and compound heterozygous rapsyn mutations causing EP AChR deficiency myasthenic syndrome; CMS11 label is nomenclature.

checks.claim: The RAPSN gene is located on chromosome 11p11.2.
checks.evidence_quote: Rapsyn mutations in humans cause endplate acetylcholine-receptor deficiency and myasthenic syndrome.
checks.explanation: Chromosomal location is standard nomenclature not stated in the abstract; accepted as nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: CMS11 is an autosomal recessive congenital myasthenic syndrome in which mutations in the RAPSN gene cause endplate acetylcholine receptor (AChR) deficiency (Ohno et al., 2002). Rapsyn, a 43-kD postsynaptic protein, plays an essential role in clustering AChR at the endplate (Ohno et al., 2002). Burke et al. (2003) distinguished early- and late-onset phenotypes. In their review, Engel et al. (2015) stated that most patients present in the first year of life. Nearly one-third have arthrogryposis at birth and other congenital malformations, and intercurrent infections or fever can trigger respiratory crises. Engel et al. (2015) described a milder phenotype with facial malformations in Near-Eastern Jewish patients homozygous for a promoter E-box mutation.

paragraphs.text: Goldhammer et al. (1990) described 14 Jewish patients from 10 families of Iraqi or Iranian origin who had congenital myasthenia with facial malformations. The malformations included an elongated face, mandibular prognathism with class III malocclusion, and a high-arched palate. Muscle weakness was mainly restricted to ptosis, weakness of the facial and masticatory muscles, and fatigable speech. The course was mild and nonprogressive, and the patients responded to cholinesterase inhibitors. Antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor were absent. Repetitive nerve stimulation at 3 Hz gave a decremental response, but a single nerve stimulus produced no repetitive compound muscle action potential.

paragraphs.text: Das et al. (2014) reported a 20-month-old boy with rapsyn deficiency. At birth he had a weak cry, hypotonia, joint contractures, and facial deformity. Because of respiratory difficulty associated with muscle fatigue, he spent a total of 71 days in the neonatal intensive care unit and 47 days in the pediatric intensive care unit. Imaging, a battery of metabolic tests, and electrodiagnostic studies were normal. Muscle biopsy showed myofiber atrophy in a pattern consistent with early denervation.

paragraphs.text: Ohno et al. (2002) studied 4 patients with endplate AChR deficiency who had no mutations in AChR subunit genes and identified 3 recessive mutations in the RAPSN gene. One patient was compound heterozygous for L14P in tetratricopeptide repeat 1 (TPR1) and N88K in TPR3. Two were homozygous for N88K. One carried N88K and 553ins5, which causes a frameshift in TPR5. Endplate studies in each patient showed decreased staining for rapsyn and AChR and impaired postsynaptic morphologic development. Expression studies in HEK cells showed that none of the mutations impaired rapsyn self-association, but all 3 reduced coclustering of AChR with rapsyn.

paragraphs.text: Ohno et al. (2003) identified 2 E-box mutations in the RAPSN promoter region in 8 patients with congenital myasthenic syndrome. Patient 1 carried a -27C-G mutation that changes an E-box at -27 to -22 from CAGCTG to GAGCTG. The allele carrying this mutation was not transcribed in the patient's muscle. Patients 2 through 8 were Oriental Jews of Iraqi or Iranian origin with facial malformations. They carried a -38A-G mutation that changes another E-box at -40 to -35 from CAACTG to CAGCTG without affecting the consensus CANNTG sequence. In electrophoretic mobility shift assays, -38A-G gained, and -27C-G lost, binding affinity for different components of nuclear extracts of C2C12 myotubes. In luciferase reporter assays, both mutations attenuated reporter gene expression in C2C12 myotubes. The -27C-G mutation also attenuated expression in HEK cells transfected with MyoD or myogenin, and it markedly attenuated the enhancer activity of an E-box on an SV40 promoter. Ohno et al. (2003) concluded that impaired transcription from the RAPSN promoter region predicts reduced rapsyn expression and endplate AChR deficiency.

paragraphs.text: Engel et al. (2015) reviewed the functions of rapsyn. Rapsyn concentrates and anchors AChR in the postsynaptic membrane and is required for development of the junctional folds. They reported that in rapsyn deficiency, multiple synaptic contacts appear on single muscle fibers. The endplate AChR deficiency is milder than in primary AChR deficiency, and the junctional folds are not well differentiated. Multiple small nerve terminals lie over poorly developed junctional folds, and AChR is distributed patchily on the postsynaptic membrane. According to Engel et al. (2015), different mutations hinder rapsyn self-association or binding to AChR, impede agrin-MuSK-LRP4-mediated clustering of AChR, or decrease rapsyn expression.
